text.p: A pro-government demonstration aimed at propping up Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was dwarfed on Tuesday by a rival opposition rally after fierce street battles in which a man was shot in the head.

The violence died down while the demonstrations were under way but erupted again in darkness after a march in central Belgrade by over 200,000 supporters of the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties.
Riot police fired teargas and made baton charges against demonstrators who pelted them with sticks and fireworks, but appeared to be acting with restraint.

Only 40,000 Socialist (SPS) supporters, a fraction of those expected, turned out for a pro-government rally, a blow to Milosevic's attempts to quell 35 days of protests by opposition Zajedno (Together) parties who accuse him of election fraud.
In his first public appearance since the crisis began, Milosevic warned: "Noone will be allowed to destabilise Serbia."
The SPS decision to hold its rally outside Zajedno's headquarters at the same time as the daily opposition demonstration plunged the city centre into chaos.
Rival groups among the crowds converging on the venue fought running battles with sticks and iron bars and a gunman who fired from a group of SPS supporters seriously injured a young man in the head.
Independent media said seven people were treated for knife wounds and several police were reported hurt.
Police separated the two sets of demonstrators but took an hour to push the Zajedno supporters 100 metres (yards) from the stand erected for Milosevic's speech.
The violence was the first since Zajedno began its protests against Milosevic's suppression of its victories in local elections on November 17.
The SPS brought thousands of supporters, many rumoured to be armed, under police escort from all over Serbia in what opposition sources condemned as a clear provocation.
There were fears the authorities would use the violence as an excuse to ban future demonstrations or even to declare a state of emergency.

Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic told supporters: "Milosevic has clearly turned full circle and has gone back to provoking disturbances. Belgrade was quiet until he brought his supporters here. The minute they came, the shooting began."
Milosevic, under threat of Western reprisals, had not previously used his police against the demonstrations, the biggest since 1992 when he used tanks to quell unrest.

Zajedno has received Western support for its campaign to force Milosevic to concede opposition victories in Belgrade and 14 other towns at the municipal elections, breaking half a century of socialist rule.
The first SPS suporters began jeering outside Zajedno headquarters three hours before the party's demonstration was due to begin.
Opposition sources said the troublemakers were from Pec, a hardline nationalist redoubt in the southern republic of Kosovo.
Kosovo Serbs were the shock troops who brought Milosevic to power on a tide of nationalism that set off the disintegration of former Yugoslavia in 1991-92.

Opposition spokesman Slobodan Vuksanovic told Reuters: "(Milosevic) is out of his mind. He has brought thousands of people to Belgrade, people who are not informed about this situation ... I am afraid it could be the beginning of civil war in Serbia and all responsibility is on Milosevic's side."
As the atmosphere of intimidation grew during the morning, the SPO party -- a Zajedno partner -- said its Belgrade bookshop was attacked by a group of unidentified men, at least three of them armed.
Zajedno earlier rejected an appeal by Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Pavle to suspend its demonstration after he warned that the conflict risked turning into an armed confrontation.
In a swipe at Milosevic, he coupled his plea with praise for the opposition's restraint during the campaign of protests.
